Afterward, he goes home for dinner, works at the office until very late, and returns home for supper and bed while suffering from a severe cold he caught the previous Sunday from sitting too long bareheaded while Mercer combed his hair and washed his ears.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The Dutch decision to halt trade for eighteen months is very strange because it contradicts the common belief that they cannot sustain themselves without commerce.

salience.tether.referent: Dutch prohibition of trade for eighteen months
salience.tether.stake: war preparations contrary to expectations of Dutch economic survival

parsed.narrative.summary: After discussing Tangier business with Mr. Creed, the narrator is visited by Jane Welsh, who has left her master to be with a poor sweetheart named Harbing. He takes her by boat to a house near the Falcon and tries for an hour or two to persuade her to return to her master, though she refuses despite believing it will be her ruin. Later, he attends to various Navy and Tangier matters with Mr. Povy, Lord Bellasses, the Duke of Albemarle, and the Duke of Yorke. At White Hall, he has an engaging discussion with Mr. Slingsby regarding the Mint, money in circulation, and the folly of prohibiting the export of bullion. On his way home, he visits the ailing Sir J. Minnes and views Mrs. Turner's rock before working late at his office.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Through Mr. Slingsby's arguments, the narrator comes to fully understand that prohibiting the export of bullion is an ineffective and harmful policy, while earlier concluding that Jane Welsh's devotion to a worthless man even to her own ruin is a strange and stupid thing.

parsed.narrative.summary: Desiring to end his trouble of mind regarding the Tangier business, the narrator offered Mr. Povy the chance to become Treasurer again, which Povy strongly refused. Although initially satisfied, the narrator was put into doubt by Creed, who explained the auditors' plain reasons why Povy might be reinstated, but also provided ingenious advice to procure an order for Povy's remaining account payments. Later, the narrator dined with Creed, where they discussed the narrator's business and discovered Will Howe's dissembling and false behavior toward them. After an afternoon at White Hall and an outing to Mile-End Greene with his wife for cream and cakes, the narrator learned that morning rumors of a naval battle and Captain Teddiman losing his legs were false, leaving him heartily glad that the fleet and the Royall Katherine were well.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Securing an order for Povy to pay the remainder of his accounts will prevent the auditors' complications from being fastened upon him, and Will Howe is a very false fellow.

parsed.narrative.summary: On Saturday, the narrator spoke seriously with his boy's lute-master, threatening to turn the boy away if he did not attend to his music, and then spent a busy day at the office while receiving news that the fleet had sailed toward Holland. The next day, being the Lord's day and the King's Coronation day, he took his wife to White Hall Chapel, stopped at a tavern to chat with a modest maid, and returned to hear an exceptional sermon by the young Stillingfleete. Afterward, they dined at Mr. Povy's, where Povy's excessive self-commendation made the experience nauseous to the narrator and underwhelming for his wife. Following a coach ride in the fields beyond St. Pancras, they hosted friends at home for music and supper, during which the narrator argued with Captain Taylor about the rhythm of a Corant until Taylor was vexed, though they parted friends and the narrator and Creed laughed about it afterward before going to bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Stillingfleete delivered the most plain, honest, and substantial sermon the narrator had ever heard, whereas Povy's habit of overdoing his own praise made his hospitality nauseous.

canon.narrative.summary: The diarist takes pleasure in timing his walk to Greenwich with his minute watch before visiting Sir W. Hickes's house, which he finds ruined, miserably looked after, and offering the meanest dinner he has ever seen, save for a fine Van-Dike picture. Walking home with Mr. Pen, he is troubled to find his wife has been abroad all day into the cold evening without anyone knowing where. At supper at Pen's mother's house, his wife arrives safely after spending the day with Captain Cocke. Later, the diarist and Mr. Pen get into an hour-long dispute over the French words 'D'un air tout interdict,' becoming almost angry and breaking up unsatisfied before going to bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist woke at five in the morning full of fear of an ague, traveled by water to the Tower, and learned from the Weekly Bill that 6,878 people had died of the plague, causing him to fear its continuation. He then traveled to Brainford while reading a play, met Mr. Povy, and rode merrily to Sir R. Viner's estate at Swakely. There, Sir Robert showed them the uniform house and grounds with great respect, including a dried body of a boy in a box, followed by dinner and Mrs. Worship's daughter singing to the diarist's great delight. After concluding his chief business to his content by securing a promise of money, he had a pleasant journey back with Povy, who shared Court news about the King being unwell and out of humour, before returning by water to Woolwich at one in the morning.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The dreadful death toll in the Weekly Bill gives reason to fear that the plague has taken such hold that it will continue.

Having nowhere else to go and not wanting to show too much fear, the narrator went to bed until ten o'clock, when Cocke woke him with the joyful news that the boy was well again. Later, after dining at Lord Bruncker's and doing office business, the narrator visited Sir J. Minnes's house, where a great feud and disorder arose over supper etiquette involving the Battens and Mr. Boreman. Because of the lingering disorder from both the feud and the earlier illness of Cocke's boy, the narrator was forced to seek other lodging and stayed comfortably in W. Hewer's room in town.
canon.narrative.meaning: The narrator concluded that it was not fitting to show too much fear by leaving Cocke's house immediately, especially since he had nowhere else to go at that hour.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist arrived at the fleet and boarded the Prince, where a £5,000 bargain for goods was agreed, though he felt great cause to be glad that he escaped signing for the whole sum upon reflecting on Captain Cocke's craft and condition. After dining and visiting Sir W. Pen and Lord Sandwich, he and his companions took a wherry toward Chatham in the calm weather. As it grew dark in a wild place, they were put to great difficulties and mightily vexed because their waterman did not know the way and an odd fisher-boy they picked up would not answer aloud. Despite this, they were surprised by the seawater seeming like fire at every oar stroke, and the boy carried them safely to Rochester, where they supped at the Crowne Inne, made themselves merry with the boy's story, and went to bed in their clothes.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Escaping the obligation to guarantee the £5,000 payment was fortunate given Captain Cocke's craft and uncertain financial condition.

Afterward, the diarist goes with Lord Bruncker aboard the Bezan to examine W. Howe, finding him unexpectedly witty, cunning, and well-spoken during the trial. He reflects on how afflictions have left Howe so subjected and dejected that he flatters the diarist in letters as "My Honour," before returning to his office to write letters late into the night.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Afflictions can leave a man so subjected and dejected that he resorts to excessive flattery.

salience.tether.stake: being out of bonds for my Lord and observing a colleague under affliction

At the office, he found Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten returned from their week-long absences at Chatham and Harwich. At noon, he went by water with his wife and Mr. Moore to Chelsea regarding his Privy Seal for Tangier, but the Lord Privy Seal was out, forcing them to return without leaving the boat. He then went with Sir Philip Warwicke to the Lord Treasurer, who signed his commission as Tangier-Treasurer and the docquet of his Privy Seal. After checking White Hall again without finding the Lord Privy Seal, he picked up his wife and woman at Unthanke's, worked late at his office, and went to supper and bed.
